title: US nursing-home profits are widely tunneled to related parties, changing the apparent return and regulatory picture
source_unit: US nursing-home providers, related-party real-estate and management payments, reported profits, assets, investment returns, reimbursements, and liability exposure

observations.period: Working paper issued March 2024; revised September 2025; detailed nursing-home financial data

denominator.unit: US nursing-home providers and related-party financial accounts; exact sample count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

profits_tunneled.unit: percent of nursing-home profits estimated to be tunneled to related parties

reported_investment_irr.unit: percent implied typical investment internal rate of return before accounting for tunneled profits and assets

adjusted_investment_irr.unit: percent implied typical investment internal rate of return after accounting for tunneled profits and assets

related_party_route.unit: inflated payments to commonly-owned related real-estate and management companies

regulatory_risk.unit: understated profitability may encourage higher reimbursements and relaxed quality standards, while asset shielding may reduce malpractice liability exposure

observations.method: The paper uses uniquely detailed nursing-home financial data to identify inflated payments to commonly-owned related parties and compares reported with adjusted profits, assets, and implied investment returns.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose provider counts, time coverage, effect uncertainty, or the full identification and accounting assumptions. The estimate is a working-paper result; tunneling evidence does not by itself establish illegal conduct, resident harm, worker harm, reimbursement changes, or causal quality effects.
observations.subgroup: Nursing-home providers with commonly-owned related real-estate or management entities.
observations.counterinterpretation: Related-party payments can include legitimate services, risk allocation, financing, tax, ownership, or accounting choices; the adjusted return depends on classification and valuation assumptions, and profit extraction does not identify the care, staffing, pricing, or resident-outcome response.

related_sources.claim: Nursing-home acquisitions reduce deficiency citations but also direct-care hours without meaningful resident-health improvement.
Inspection responses are mostly temporary, while higher ratings predict relative patient mortality.
California nursing homes manipulate size around a staffing threshold, limiting access particularly for disadvantaged patients.

boundary: This record adds a financial-governance layer to the US nursing-home chain. It does not establish illegality, resident or worker harm, reimbursement fraud, clinical quality effects, prices, access, or causal links between tunneling and care outcomes in the same unit.
